oldVerdictReview.reason: Reviewed the three copied exact original Culture/Nature causal examples: policy or educational opportunity does not establish comparative inherited-versus-social causal beliefs, and unsupported competing claims cannot produce Neutral. This supports material withdrawal without claiming all old answers wrong or using new nulls as proof.

reviewedExamples.oldRationale: Qualified agreement with the proposition concerning upbringing outweighing inherited tendencies in general behaviour. Cultural evolution and acquired rules shape conduct alongside inherited instincts and biological capacities. Evolution of institutions must not be confused with genetic transmission of each social outcome. This is a low-confidence causal analogy; the claim is about explanatory emphasis, not a scientific estimate or a consequence of equal moral worth.
reviewedExamples.finding: Missing personal evidence within 1944–1988 resolving upbringing greater than inherited general behaviour. Normative equality, schooling policy, learned conventions or recognition that genes and environment interact do not establish the comparative causal claim.

reviewedExamples.oldRationale: Qualified disagreement with the proposition concerning inherited national differences outweighing education in IQ scores. Cultural evolution and acquired rules shape conduct alongside inherited instincts and biological capacities. Evolution of institutions must not be confused with genetic transmission of each social outcome. This is a low-confidence causal analogy; the claim is about explanatory emphasis, not a scientific estimate or a consequence of equal moral worth.
reviewedExamples.finding: Missing personal evidence within 1944–1988 resolving inherited national IQ differences greater than education. Normative equality, schooling policy, learned conventions or recognition that genes and environment interact do not establish the comparative causal claim.

reviewedExamples.oldRationale: Hayek distinguishes evolved cultural rules from inherited capacities rather than reducing one to the other. Applied to sex-differentiated conduct, social opportunities and family expectations counts on one side and embodied differences on the other. The neutral assessment expresses that interaction, not a claim that the subject made a modern quantitative comparison. Confidence in this particular analogy is low.

oldVerdictReview.reason: Reviewed the three copied exact original Culture/Nature causal examples: policy or educational opportunity does not establish comparative inherited-versus-social causal beliefs, and unsupported competing claims cannot produce Neutral. This supports material withdrawal without claiming all old answers wrong or using new nulls as proof.

reviewedExamples.oldRationale: Rawls distinguishes natural endowments from the social conditions in which abilities develop. Applied to general conduct, incentives and upbringing counts on one side and natural capacities on the other. The neutral assessment expresses that interaction, not a claim that the subject made a modern quantitative comparison. Confidence in this particular analogy is low.
reviewedExamples.finding: Missing personal evidence within 1971–2001 resolving upbringing greater than inherited general behaviour. Normative equality, schooling policy, learned conventions or recognition that genes and environment interact do not establish the comparative causal claim.

reviewedExamples.oldRationale: Rawls distinguishes natural endowments from the social conditions in which abilities develop. Applied to national IQ differences, schooling and educational opportunity counts on one side and individual cognitive endowments, which cannot automatically be aggregated into national heredity on the other. The neutral assessment expresses that interaction, not a claim that the subject made a modern quantitative comparison. Confidence in this particular analogy is low.
reviewedExamples.finding: Missing personal evidence within 1971–2001 resolving inherited national IQ differences greater than education. Normative equality, schooling policy, learned conventions or recognition that genes and environment interact do not establish the comparative causal claim.

reviewedExamples.oldRationale: Qualified agreement with the proposition concerning social expectations outweighing biology in sex differences. Natural endowments and social circumstances both affect life prospects; institutions influence how talents develop. Moral arbitrariness of birth does not determine a genetic-versus-cultural causal percentage. This is a low-confidence causal analogy; the claim is about explanatory emphasis, not a scientific estimate or a consequence of equal moral worth.
reviewedExamples.finding: Missing personal evidence within 1971–2001 resolving social causes greater than biological sex behaviour. Normative equality, schooling policy, learned conventions or recognition that genes and environment interact do not establish the comparative causal claim.
